title: A performance refactor of AdminPermission.projects split one combined Q filter into chained .filter(teams__members=user).filter(teams__access=ADMIN_ACCESS) calls, so read-only team members get admin rights on any project that also belongs to some admin team.

findings.explanation: The code uses Django ORM query builders (Project.objects.filter(), .exclude()) with field lookups and Q objects. No user-controlled input is directly concatenated into SQL queries. The parameters are passed through Django's parameterization layer.

The logic change modifies how projects are filtered based on admin/member flags. The original code used OR logic (filter |=) to include projects where the user has EITHER ADMIN_ACCESS OR READ_ONLY_ACCESS in teams. The new code changes this: when both admin=True and member=True, it skips filtering by access level entirely (just passes), returning all projects where the user is a team member regardless of their access role. This represents a potential authorization bypass - users could gain access to projects they shouldn't if both flags are somehow set to True together, violating the principle of least privilege. The condition `if admin and not member` / `elif member and not admin` suggests the code assumes these are mutually exclusive, but the else clause that does no filtering could be exploited if both are true.
findings.suggested_fix: Clarify the intended behavior when both admin and member are True. If they should be mutually exclusive, add an assertion or explicit error. If both being true is valid, explicitly define what access levels should be included (e.g., filter for both ADMIN_ACCESS OR READ_ONLY_ACCESS). The current pass statement silently returns all team projects without access-level filtering.
